### Epistocracy and Constitutions

##### Udit Bhatia Linacre College

Thesis submitted in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of DPhil in Politics at the Department of Politics and International Relations at the University of Oxford

#### Abstract

Recently, some political commentators and academics have suggested that we should replace democracy with ‘epistocracy’, or rule by the competent. Drawing on historical case studies in Britain, India and the United States, the first part of this thesis sheds light on the use of franchise restrictions, legislative office qualifications, and indirect elections as epistocratic mechanisms concerned with competence in the legislative assembly. The second part of the thesis offers a normative critique of each of these mechanisms, demonstrating why these would be either self-defeating or simply futile from an epistemic perspective.

#### Acknowledgements

This thesis would not have been possible, quite literally, without Liz Frazer. Early

philosophically pressing in our time than the conflict between democracy and rule by 
experts. She highlighted the value of remaining ambitious, incorporating a historical

Working on this thesis has reminded me that our academic work is as much

I cannot express adequate gratitude for my family. My parents, my sister and my

#### Introduction

On 9

th

November 2016, I was scheduled to teach a class for undergraduate students on justifications for democracy. It so happened, without planning for this, that the class coincided with the morning on which the results of the United States presidential elections were announced. Faced with the reality of Donald Trump’s election, my students seemed to have changed their minds about whether all citizens ought to have a vote. Having defended the right to vote in their essays, written some days before the American election, they had shown much more faith in democratic institutions. Now, many had changed their minds. In many ways, this was similar to the reactions found to the vote on Britain’s membership of the European Union earlier that year. One set of critics claimed that a question like this ought never to have been decided through a referendum. However, much of the criticism went beyond the appropriateness of a referendum and focused instead on the ‘stupidity’ or ‘incompetence’ of voters. All around, the idea that all voters must first have to undergo some sort of competence test had become more popular than I had ever imagined.

1

The idea, however, was not an unfamiliar one. Growing up in India I had long been told that much of the problems that plagued society were a function of illiterate persons. On such accounts, illiterate voters were responsible for ensuring that politics would never move beyond identity to focus on policies instead. They also suggested that incompetent and criminal persons would be elected to legislative office as long as illiterate persons exercised a vote.

2

Arguments such as these in India had motivated my interest in the nexus between competence and democratic institutions. But they had, by the time I started writing this thesis, become part of public discourse elsewhere too.
